title: From Penha to Lapa: the Arena, the Cells, and the Theatre of the Oppressed
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Penha, and the Chemistry That Did Not Take

stops.name: Penha, Rio de Janeiro: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; 16 March 1931 is confirmed independently by the English, Portuguese and Spanish Wikipedia articles. The gathering pass gave the birthplace as Penha Circular and that is struck as anachronistic: Penha Circular was constituted a distinct bairro only on 23 July 1981, fifty years later.
stops.campa: In the subúrbio da Penha, north of the city centre, a son is born to José Augusto Boal and Albertina Pinto, Portuguese immigrants. They name him Augusto Pinto Boal. The Rio around the house is the Rio of the suburban train line and the factory whistle, not the Rio of the beaches, and the family speaks Portuguese with the accent of the other side of the ocean. Seventy-eight years later he will die eleven kilometres south of this street, in Botafogo, having in the interval built a theatre that is practised in prisons on four continents.
suggested_refs: The Penha bairro of Rio de Janeiro's north zone, as it stood before Penha Circular was split off from it in 1981

stops.name: Penha, Rio de Janeiro: the cousins directed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Spanish article gives only 'age ten'; the year 1941 is arithmetic from the stated age against the attested birth year, not a dated event. No source names a play, a room, or a witness.
stops.campa: At about ten he gathers the cousins and the younger siblings and puts them through plays in the house. He assigns the parts and tells them where to stand and when to come in. Nobody records what they performed. The tradition survives only as the shape of the thing: a child who arranges other people into a fiction and then watches it from outside. The definition he will publish at sixty holds that theatre requires no building at all, and he arrives at that position having started without one.
stops.quote: Theatre has nothing to do with buildings or other physical constructions. Theatre — or theatricality — is the capacity, this human property which allows man to observe himself in action, in activity.
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, The Rainbow of Desire, trans. Adrian Jackson (Routledge, 1995), p. 13
suggested_refs: The Boal family house in Penha, site of the earliest reported productions

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the Universidade do Brasil: chemical engineering
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the gathering pass tagged this attested and the tag is demoted. The Portuguese article gives only 'age seventeen', so 1948 is arithmetic. Two corrections carried: the institution was the antiga Universidade do Brasil, renamed UFRJ only in 1965, and the field was engenharia química, not chemistry. The 1948 location of the Escola Nacional de Química is not established by any reachable source, so the pin sits on central Rio.
stops.campa: At seventeen he enrols in chemical engineering at the Universidade do Brasil, which will not be called the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro for another seventeen years. He takes the degree at about twenty-one. He is good at it. He goes on writing plays through the whole course, and when he sails for New York it is nominally to continue with the chemistry, which is what he tells his father. The laboratory leaves one mark on the method he later builds: it is organised as a sequence of exercises, run, observed, adjusted, and written up.
suggested_refs: The Escola Nacional de Química of the Universidade do Brasil, before the move to the Ilha do Fundão campus

segments.name: Columbia, Gassner, and the Writer's Group

stops.name: New York, Columbia University: the switch to dramatic arts
stops.date_confidence: substance attested, year reconstructed. Both the English and Portuguese articles say only 'the 1950s' for the Columbia period; the gathering pass fixed it at 1953 and tagged it attested, which overstates the evidence. Columbia, the switch to dramatic arts, and John Gassner are attested by both articles.
stops.campa: He arrives to study chemical engineering and finds John Gassner, the critic, teaching dramatic arts, and changes course. Gassner puts Brecht and Stanislavski in front of him in the same year: the one who wants the audience awake and calculating, the other who wants the actor inhabited. Boal spends fifty years refusing to choose between them, and builds a form in which the audience does the inhabiting. He also sits in at the Actors Studio, watching American actors take a scene apart as though it were a machine with removable parts.
suggested_refs: John Gassner's dramatic arts teaching at Columbia in the 1950s, the point of Boal's turn

stops.name: New York: the Actors Studio on West 44th Street
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The English and Portuguese articles both attest attendance at the Actors Studio during the 1950s Columbia period, and neither gives a year; 1954 is a placement between the arrival and the 1955 productions.
stops.campa: The Studio on West 44th Street, under Lee Strasberg, is where the Method is being made in public. Boal watches, and takes from the room the conviction that acting is a technique rather than a gift, and therefore teachable in steps to anybody. If it can be taught to a professional it can be taught to a metalworker or to a prisoner, and the professional loses his monopoly on the stage. He is a Brazilian chemistry student among people who believe that theatre is a craft.
suggested_refs: The Actors Studio at 432 West 44th Street, New York, in the years of Strasberg's directorship

stops.name: New York: the plays staged with the Writer's Group
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1955 by the English article, which groups 'The Horse and the Saint' with 'The House Across the Street' in that year. The Spanish article's looser Writer's Group narrative implies 1954 for 'The House Across the Street'. The contradiction is printed here, not resolved. No month; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: With Columbia's Writer's Group he writes and stages two of his own: The Horse and the Saint, and The House Across the Street. They are the first Boal plays to reach an audience, and they reach it in English, in a country he is only passing through. Nothing in them announces the Teatro do Oprimido, and nobody reading them afterwards has found the method waiting in them. What they establish is that the chemistry is finished. He is twenty-four, he holds a degree he will never use, and São Paulo is about to send for him.
suggested_refs: The scripts of 'The Horse and the Saint' and 'The House Across the Street', Boal's earliest staged work

stops.name: São Paulo, the Teatro de Arena: the invitation
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1956 by the English and Portuguese articles, the latter naming Sábato Magaldi and José Renato as the men who invited him. The Spanish article dates the entry to 1955 and has him assume the artistic direction on arrival; both of those claims are set aside as unsupported by the other two editions, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than deleted. No month; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Sábato Magaldi and José Renato call him to a small theatre on the Rua Teodoro Baima with the stage in the middle and the audience on all four sides. There is no proscenium here and no fourth wall to break, because there is no wall. The room seats a couple of hundred and the company is broke. He comes in as a director, not as head of the house; the artistic direction follows later. For the next fifteen years the Arena is where Brazilian theatre argues with itself, and he is standing in the middle of the argument.
suggested_refs: The Teatro de Arena on Rua Teodoro Baima, Vila Buarque, São Paulo, the first theatre in the round in Brazil

stops.name: São Paulo, the Teatro de Arena: Ratos e Homens and the first prize
stops.date_confidence: the year 1956 is attested: the Portuguese article names 'Ratos e Homens' as his first production at the Arena that year, and the English article records the Direction Revelation Award for it. No month is given by either; June is a placement inside the attested year to keep this stop after the arrival.
stops.campa: His first production at the Arena is Steinbeck, Of Mice and Men, played in Portuguese as Ratos e Homens: two migrant labourers on the road with nothing, one of them shot at the end by the only person who loves him. It takes him the Direction Revelation Award. The choice of text is already the argument he will be making for the rest of his life. Working men stand on a bare stage, in the round, in a country whose theatre still mostly imports its drawing rooms from Paris.
suggested_refs: The 1956 Arena production of 'Ratos e Homens' and the Prêmio Revelação de Direção

stops.name: São Paulo, the Teatro de Arena: the classics reset in Brazil
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the English article describes this as a practice of the Arena years and does not date it. 1957 is a placement inside the period, between the 1956 arrival and the 1958 seminar. No month; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He moves the classical repertoire onto Brazilian ground: the plot kept, the setting changed, the actors trained in Stanislavski so that they play their own country instead of an imported one. The company learns to work from what its members actually know. The decision is technical and small. Once the actor's own life is the material, what stands between the actor and the person watching is no longer a wall but a step, and a step can be taken in either direction.
suggested_refs: The Arena's programme of nationalising the classical repertoire, 1957 onward

stops.name: São Paulo: the Seminário de Dramaturgia
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1958 by the Spanish article, which names Gianfrancesco Guarnieri as co-founder. No month given; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: With Gianfrancesco Guarnieri he opens a dramaturgy seminar inside the theatre: a workshop in which the company writes the plays it will perform instead of buying them. Brazilian authors write on Brazilian subjects, and the company reads the drafts aloud and pulls them apart in front of the actors who will have to speak the lines. The Arena stops being a house that stages other people's texts and becomes a place that manufactures them. A good share of the Brazilian playwrights of the following decade pass through the room.
suggested_refs: The Seminário de Dramaturgia of the Teatro de Arena, founded 1958 with Gianfrancesco Guarnieri

stops.name: São Paulo: Chapetuba Futebol Clube
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1959 by the English article, which names Oduvaldo Vianna Filho as the author. No month; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He directs Oduvaldo Vianna Filho's play about a small-town football club, a fixed match, and the men who are paid to lose it. It comes straight out of the seminar: a Brazilian author writing about Brazilian money and Brazilian shame, staged in the round for an audience close enough to touch the players. Vianna Filho is in his early twenties. Within five years the men who make this kind of theatre will be enemies of the state, and within twelve Boal will be taken off a São Paulo street.
suggested_refs: Oduvaldo Vianna Filho, 'Chapetuba Futebol Clube', Teatro de Arena, 1959

stops.name: São Paulo: Revolução na América do Sul
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1960 by the Spanish article, which gives the title as 'Revolución en América del Sur'. No month; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He writes one of his own: a comic epic about José da Silva, the average Brazilian, starving his way through one political solution after another, each of which explains to him why he is not hungry. It is Brecht rebuilt in the register of the carnival and the radio serial. The play travels, and it is the first Boal text through which people outside Brazil learn his name. He is twenty-nine and he has found the tone he keeps, which is that the joke and the accusation are one sentence.
suggested_refs: Augusto Boal, 'Revolução na América do Sul' (1960), his first widely circulated play

stops.name: Brasília: the coup of 1964
stops.date_confidence: the year 1964 is attested by the English article as the coup that begins the dictatorship under which Boal is later persecuted; the article gives no day, and 1 April is the conventional date of the completed takeover. No source in the pool places Boal anywhere in particular that week. The pin is the seat of the government overthrown, not his position.
stops.campa: The military take the government. What follows lasts twenty-one years and reaches Boal in stages: censorship first, then the loss of the audiences, then, seven years in, a car and a hood. Paulo Freire, who is teaching the same country to read by asking it which words it already carries, is expelled this year and stays abroad for sixteen. The educator and the director are building the same instrument from opposite ends, and the coup is what sends both of them to build it somewhere else.
suggested_refs: The Brazilian coup d'état of 1964 and the expulsion of Paulo Freire in the same year

stops.name: São Paulo, the Teatro de Arena: the Arena Conta series begins
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1965 by the Spanish article, which dates the start of the 'Arena Conta' series of historical-political musicals and names Guarnieri as collaborator. The article names no individual titles and none are supplied. No month; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Under censorship a company cannot say what it means about the present, so Boal and Guarnieri say it about the past. The Arena Conta plays are historical musicals: a rebellion centuries old, sung, with the songs written by living composers and the parallel left for the audience to draw. The trick is ancient and it works, because a censor must either pass the play or state in writing what the history resembles. Boal works this seam for six more years, until the state stops bothering with censors.
suggested_refs: The 'Arena Conta' cycle of historical musicals, begun 1965 with Gianfrancesco Guarnieri

stops.name: São Paulo: the musicals and the singers
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1968 by the English article, which records musical theatre works featuring major Brazilian popular-music artists. The article names no artists and none are supplied here. The Feira Paulista de Opinião of the same year is attested by the Portuguese article by way of its 2018 revival. No month; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He makes musical theatre with the biggest popular singers in the country, in the year the regime issues Institutional Act Number Five and closes what was left of the opening. The audience for a Boal show is now the audience for a record, which is to say a national one, and the state notices. The same year he mounts the Primeira Feira Paulista de Opinião, a survey of what Brazilian writers think about Brazil, which is exactly the kind of question about to become illegal to ask in public.
suggested_refs: The Primeira Feira Paulista de Opinião, São Paulo, 1968, revived by Clarice Boal in 2018

stops.name: São Paulo: taken off the street
stops.date_confidence: the year 1971 is attested by both the English and Spanish articles; neither gives a month, a day, a street, or the unit that made the arrest. Month and day default to 01 and the pin is the city rather than a site. The detention facility is a stated gap: OBAN, DOPS and DOI-CODI are the candidates a reader will expect and none is named by any source in the pool.
stops.campa: Agents of the military government take him off a São Paulo street. The English account uses the word kidnapped, which is the accurate one: no warrant, no charge read out, no record of where he has gone. He is a director of musicals with famous singers in them, and the state has classified him as a subversive cultural activist, which in Brazil in 1971 is a category with a building attached and a set of instruments inside it. His family does not know for some time whether he is alive.
suggested_refs: The 1971 arrest of Augusto Boal; no detention facility is named in any reachable source

stops.name: São Paulo: the torture
stops.date_confidence: the year 1971 is attested by the English article, which states plainly that he was kidnapped and tortured by agents of the regime. No facility, month, day or duration is given by any source in the pool; March is a placement inside the attested year, after the arrest and before the departure. The pin is the city.
stops.campa: They torture him. He survives it, and afterwards he writes about torture rather than about himself: a play set in the Inquisition, whose interrogators use the arguments the Brazilian ones use. Everything he builds from here has that room somewhere inside it. The Theatre of the Oppressed does not ask an audience to feel sorry for a victim. It stops the scene and asks what the person on stage could have done instead, which is the question a man puts to himself for years about a room he was not able to leave.
stops.quote: To resist, it is not enough to say No – it is necessary to desire!
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, The Aesthetics of the Oppressed, trans. Adrian Jackson (Routledge, 2006)
suggested_refs: Augusto Boal, 'Torquemada' (1971), written out of the torture and set in the Spanish Inquisition

stops.name: São Paulo: released into exile
stops.date_confidence: the year 1971 is attested by the English and Spanish articles for the arrest, the torture and the departure into Argentine exile; the sequence is attested, the interval between the three is not. June is a placement inside the year to hold the order, not a dated event.
stops.campa: He is let go and he leaves. Brazil will not have him back for fifteen years. He goes south to Buenos Aires carrying a method that at this point is a set of exercises and a habit of asking an audience what it would do differently; he returns with a book in more than twenty-five languages and practitioners on four continents. Exile is what turns a São Paulo director into an international one, and the regime that arranges it believes it is removing him.
suggested_refs: The fifteen-year exclusion of Boal from Brazil, 1971 to 1986

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the first exile
stops.date_confidence: the year 1971 is attested by both the English and Spanish articles for the move to Argentina; no month is given, and September is a placement after the attested arrest and release of the same year. The coordinates are the canonical Buenos Aires pin already used by isabel_peron.journey.json, spinetta.journey.json and che_guevara.journey.json, inherited byte-identically.
stops.campa: He settles in Buenos Aires, in a city Luis Alberto Spinetta left in March of this same year for seven months of his own exile through Brazil, the United States and Europe. The two do not meet in the record. Boal has five years here, and the method is assembled in them: he works out of Argentina and travels the continent, running workshops with people who are not actors and writing down what happens when they are handed the stage and told to fix the scene themselves.
suggested_refs: The Argentine exile of 1971 to 1976, the period in which the Theatre of the Oppressed is assembled

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Torquemada
stops.date_confidence: the year 1971 is attested by the English article, which places the publication of 'Torquemada' in the Argentine exile. No month is given; December is a placement inside the year, after the arrival.
stops.campa: He publishes Torquemada, a play about the systematic torture practised in Brazilian prisons, named for the Grand Inquisitor of Spain. He has been out of the cells for months. The displacement is deliberate and it is the same move he made under censorship at the Arena: put the present into a costume old enough to be printable and let the audience perform the recognition. This time he is writing from outside the country, with no censor left to satisfy, and he does it that way regardless.
suggested_refs: Augusto Boal, 'Torquemada' (Buenos Aires, 1971)

stops.name: Lima: the continental workshops
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the weakest pin in this file. The English summary of the exile years names Peru and Ecuador among the countries worked in, and the Spanish article attests continent-wide development of the techniques from Argentina between 1971 and 1976. No source in the verified pool attests a Peruvian city, date or programme name. Lima and 1973 are placements, not documents, and should be treated as such.
stops.campa: The Spanish account has him working the whole continent out of Argentina in these years; the English summary names Peru and Ecuador among the countries. What is being assembled in these workshops is the substitution that defines the method: the person watching stops watching, walks up, takes the part, and tries a different solution in front of everyone else. Boal calls the result the spect-actor. In September of this year the Chilean army takes La Moneda and Augusto Pinochet begins seventeen years of the thing these exercises rehearse against.
stops.quote: Theatre of the Oppressed is theatre in this most archaic application of the word. In this usage, all human beings are actors (they act!) and spectators (they observe!). They are spect-actors.
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, Games for Actors and Non-Actors, trans. Adrian Jackson, 2nd ed. (Routledge, 2002), p. 15
suggested_refs: The Peruvian and Ecuadorean workshops of the exile years, undocumented in any reachable source

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Ediciones de la Flor: the book
stops.date_confidence: 1974 is attested by the Open Library catalogue record for the first edition, 'Teatro del oprimido y otras poéticas políticas', Ediciones de la Flor, Buenos Aires. The English article's 1973 and the French article's 1971 are both wrong and are recorded here so that neither is reintroduced. The Portuguese edition follows in 1975, the French in 1980, the English in 1993. No month; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: The book comes out in Spanish, in Buenos Aires, from Ediciones de la Flor: Teatro del oprimido y otras poéticas políticas. It opens by attacking Aristotle, whose catharsis it reads as a machine for making an audience discharge its anger safely and then go home quiet. Against that Boal sets a theatre which refuses the discharge and hands the audience the stage. Twenty-five languages follow over the decades. The Portuguese edition waits until 1975, so the country the book is about reads it last.
stops.quote: In its most archaic sense, theatre is the capacity possessed by human beings—and not by animals—to observe themselves in action.
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, Games for Actors and Non-Actors, trans. Adrian Jackson, 1st ed. (Routledge, 1992), p. xxvi
sources: Open Library catalogue record, Ediciones de la Flor first edition, 1974
suggested_refs: Augusto Boal, 'Teatro del oprimido y otras poéticas políticas', Ediciones de la Flor, Buenos Aires, 1974

stops.name: Aeroparque Jorge Newbery, Buenos Aires: the second coup
stops.date_confidence: attested. The date, place and coordinates are carried byte-identically from isabel_peron.journey.json, which attests the fall of Isabel Perón's government at the Aeroparque on 24 March 1976. That Boal's departure from Argentina follows from this coup is inference, drawn from the Spanish article's dating of his relocation to 1976, and is not stated in that file.
stops.campa: The military take Isabel Perón at the Aeroparque, and Argentina begins its own dictatorship twelve years after Brazil began his. Boal, exiled here since 1971, is a Brazilian subversive living in a country that has just acquired the apparatus for dealing with subversives, much of it built by decree by the government being overthrown. Charly García stays and works through the whole of it. Boal packs. This second exile is the one that carries the method to Europe.
suggested_refs: The Argentine coup of 24 March 1976 and the Operativo Independencia decrees that preceded it

stops.name: Lisbon: the second exile
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1976 by the Spanish article. The English article contradicts this by describing 1971 to 1986 as one continuous exile spent in Peru, Ecuador and France, mentioning neither Argentina nor Portugal as distinct stops. The Spanish itinerary is followed here because it is the more granular; the contradiction is unresolved. No month; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He crosses to Portugal, which two years earlier removed its own dictatorship with carnations in the rifle barrels, and which is the only country in his language where a Brazilian subversive can work in the open. He has two years here. It is the first time since 1971 that he lives somewhere the state is not the problem. The Portuguese edition of the book is a year old, the readers are already here, and the method starts being taught by people who did not learn it from him.
suggested_refs: The Portuguese period of the exile, 1976 to 1978, absent from the English-language account

stops.name: Paris: the Sorbonne
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Spanish article gives 1978 for the Sorbonne invitation, and the item is tagged as reconstruction in the verified pool because no document supports it. No month; day defaults to 01. The coordinates are the canonical Paris pin already used by gilles_deleuze.journey.json and spinetta.journey.json, inherited byte-identically.
stops.campa: The Sorbonne invites him to teach the Theatre of the Oppressed. He arrives in a Paris where Gilles Deleuze has been teaching at Vincennes for ten years and Michel Foucault has been running the Groupe d'Information sur les Prisons since 1971, a city arguing about prisons, asylums and who is permitted to speak. Boal's contribution to the argument is not a book about power. It is a set of exercises that can be run in a room in two hours by somebody who has read nothing.
stops.quote: Theatre is a form of knowledge; it should and can also be a means of transforming society.
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, Games for Actors and Non-Actors, trans. Adrian Jackson, 1st ed. (Routledge, 1992), p. xxxi
suggested_refs: The Sorbonne teaching invitation of 1978, attested only in the Spanish-language account

stops.name: Paris: the Centre du Théâtre de l'Opprimé
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1979 by the Spanish article, which gives the founding name as Centre d'étude et de diffusion des techniques actives d'expression and the later name as Centre du Théâtre de l'Opprimé. No month; day defaults to 01. The Maspero edition of 1980 named in the campa is attested by the verified pool's edition chain.
stops.campa: He founds the Centre d'étude et de diffusion des techniques actives d'expression, a name long enough to disarm anyone's suspicion, later renamed for what it actually is: the Centre du Théâtre de l'Opprimé. Paris is where the method stops being Latin American. The French edition of the book comes out from Maspero in 1980, and the technique starts appearing in European classrooms, unions and psychiatric wards, run by people addressing oppressions Boal never had in view.
sources: Open Library and pool edition chain for 'Théâtre de l'opprimé', Maspero, 1980
suggested_refs: The Centre du Théâtre de l'Opprimé, Paris, founded 1979 and still operating

stops.name: Paris: the first International Festival of the Theatre of the Oppressed
stops.date_confidence: the year 1981 is attested by the English article, which does not say where the festival was held. Paris is inferred from the Centre founded there two years earlier, and the inference is flagged rather than hidden. No month; day defaults to 01. Canonical Paris pin, inherited byte-identically.
stops.campa: Practitioners come from wherever the book has reached, and for the first time the thing has a census of itself. What they bring are variants: Forum Theatre run with factory shifts, with immigrant women, with people who have been inside institutions. Boal takes the variants seriously enough to keep rewriting the exercises around them for the next twenty-eight years. The festival becomes periodic, and the method acquires the property he says he wants for it, which is not to finish.
stops.quote: Never — since the objective of Theatre of the Oppressed is not to close a cycle, to generate a catharsis or to bring an end to a process in development. On the contrary, its objective is to encourage autonomous activity, to set a process in motion, to stimulate transformative creativity, to change spectators into protagonists.
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, Games for Actors and Non-Actors, trans. Adrian Jackson, 2nd ed. (Routledge, 2002), ch. 20, p. 275
suggested_refs: The first International Festival for Theatre of the Oppressed, 1981; the source names no host city

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro: the return
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1986 by both the English and Spanish articles. Neither gives a month; month and day default to 01. The Canadian Theatre Review interview quoted here is attested to the summer of 1986 and was conducted while he was still in Europe, before the return.
stops.campa: Fifteen years after the car in São Paulo he comes home. The dictatorship has been dismantled, the country has a civilian president, and Boal is fifty-five and internationally famous for a technique nobody in Brazil has watched him practise. He begins again from the ground: workshops in the neighbourhoods, groups assembled out of whoever turns up. The same year an interviewer in Canada gets him to say what he means by the word democracy, and it turns out not to be a metaphor for the theatre.
stops.quote: I believe in democracy, but in real democracy, not a phony democracy in which just powerful people can speak. For me, in a democracy everyone speaks.
stops.quote_source: Robert Enright, 'To Dynamize the Audience: Interview with Augusto Boal,' Canadian Theatre Review 47 (Summer 1986), pp. 41-49
suggested_refs: The 1986 return to Rio de Janeiro after fifteen years of exile

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro: the Fábrica de Teatro Popular
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Spanish article attests that Boal directed the Fábrica de Teatro Popular on his return but gives it no founding date; 1986 is the year of the return and June is a placement to keep this stop after the arrival.
stops.campa: The Popular Theatre Factory is the name he gives the reentry: an outfit that carries the exercises into the parts of Rio which do not go to the theatre, and trains people there to run them without him. The word factory is the accurate one. He is not producing shows, he is producing groups, and each group can produce more groups. Every one of them is a small machine for converting an audience into people who will walk up onto a stage in front of their neighbours.
suggested_refs: The Fábrica de Teatro Popular, Rio de Janeiro, directed by Boal from 1986

stops.name: Lapa, Rio de Janeiro: the Centro de Teatro do Oprimido
stops.date_confidence: the founding year 1986 is attested directly by ctorio.org.br together with the address, Av. Mem de Sá 31, Lapa, CEP 20230-150. No month is given; December is a placement inside the attested year. The pool's longitude -43.1811 was a copy artifact duplicated from the Hospital Samaritano entry several kilometres away, and is corrected here to -43.1832 on OpenStreetMap.
stops.campa: The Centro de Teatro do Oprimido takes an address on the Avenida Mem de Sá in Lapa, under the arches, and keeps it. It is the institutional form of the whole thing: laboratories, seminars, community groups working on racial justice and on violence against women, and the archive of a method that by this point belongs to far more people than him. Four decades on it is still at the same number, which is more than can be said for most theatres and for every government he outlived.
stops.quote: O teatro foi a primeira invenção humana
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, quoted on the Centro de Teatro do Oprimido website, ctorio.org.br
sources: OpenStreetMap, Av. Mem de Sá, CEP 20230, Lapa
suggested_refs: The Centro de Teatro do Oprimido, Av. Mem de Sá 31, Lapa, Rio de Janeiro, founded 1986

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro: Somos 31 milhões, e agora?
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Spanish article dates the consolidation of CTO-Rio and this production to 1990, and the item is tagged as reconstruction in the verified pool. No month; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: The production that consolidates CTO-Rio counts the people it is addressed to and puts the number in the title: we are thirty-one million, and now what. The figure is the count of Brazilians the statistics have written off. The question mark is the method. Boal has spent twenty years refusing to end a piece with an answer, on the grounds that an answer delivered from a stage is a way of taking the problem away from the people who actually have it.
suggested_refs: 'Somos 31 milhões, e agora?', the production consolidating CTO-Rio around 1990

stops.name: Cinelândia, Rio de Janeiro: elected vereador
stops.date_confidence: the year 1992 is attested by both the English and Spanish articles for the election to the Rio city council on the Partido dos Trabalhadores ticket. Neither gives a month; the Brazilian municipal election falls in October, but since no source states it the date defaults to 01-01 rather than being invented.
stops.campa: He stands for the Rio city council on the Workers' Party ticket and wins. It is not a break from the work, it is the work moving into the building where the laws are made. The chamber is a room with a floor, a public gallery, and rules about who may speak in what order, which is to say a theatre with the spect-actors legally excluded. He arrives with fourteen years of technique built for exactly that problem, and with a memoir already forming in his head.
stops.quote: Biographies smack of the end, the final utterances. Mission accomplished. I, by contrast, am always at the start of some new path or other.
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, Hamlet and the Baker's Son: My Life in Theatre and Politics, trans. Adrian Jackson and Candida Blaker (Routledge, 2001)

stops.name: Câmara Municipal do Rio de Janeiro: Legislative Theatre
stops.date_confidence: the mandate runs January 1993 to December 1996, the standard Brazilian municipal cycle; the pool's '1993-1997' overruns by a year and is corrected. The law count is corrected too: forty bills proposed, thirteen approved during the term and four more passed later in Brasília, per the English and Portuguese articles. The pool's 'roughly fourteen' is wrong. The quote is from 2009 and is placed here for its subject, not its date.
stops.campa: Teatro Legislativo runs the method in reverse. Groups across the city stage the problem they are living, the audience intervenes, and the interventions that survive the argument are written up by his staff as draft bills and carried into the chamber. Forty are proposed. Thirteen pass during the mandate, four more later in Brasília. He does not describe this as theatre put to political use. He describes it as citizenship, and the distinction is the whole of his position.
stops.quote: We are all actors: being a citizen is not living in society, it is changing it.
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, World Theatre Day Message, International Theatre Institute, 27 March 2009

From here the honours arrive faster than he can travel to them, and they arrive from institutions rather than from the theatre: peace prizes, cultural merit, ambassadorships. He keeps running workshops throughout. The method by now is being used by people who have never heard of the Teatro de Arena and could not name a single play he wrote.

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro: the sambópera
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Spanish article dates the Carmen sambópera to 1999 and the item is tagged as reconstruction in the verified pool. No month; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He turns Carmen into a sambópera: Bizet run through the rhythm section of a Rio escola de samba, the cigarette factory and the smuggler and the knife transposed onto a country that has all three of them. It is a late instance of the oldest trick in his repertoire, the one he began at the Arena in 1957 by resetting the classics on Brazilian ground. He is sixty-eight and has been performing the same operation, on steadily larger objects, for forty-three years.

stops.name: Paris: the sambópera abroad and the prisons
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Spanish article places the Paris performance of the Carmen sambópera and the intensification of the prison work in 2000, and the item is tagged as reconstruction in the verified pool. No month; day defaults to 01. Canonical Paris pin, inherited byte-identically.
stops.campa: The Carmen goes to Paris, and in the same period he drives the Theatre of the Oppressed further into the prisons. He is running the exercises inside the one institution built specifically to stop people changing the scene they are in. He had been held in such a building himself, in São Paulo, in 1971, and had come out of it holding that a person who can rehearse an alternative is not finished. The prison workshops are that conviction taken to its address.
stops.quote: In truth, a session of Theatre of the Oppressed has no end, because everything which happens in it must extend into life. Theatre shall never end! Theatre of the Oppressed is located precisely on the frontier between fiction and reality — and this border must be crossed.
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, Games for Actors and Non-Actors, trans. Adrian Jackson, 2nd ed. (Routledge, 2002), p. 276
suggested_refs: Boal's prison work of the 2000s, in Brazil and in Europe

stops.name: Brasília: the Order of Cultural Merit
stops.date_confidence: the year 2005 is attested by the English article. No month; day defaults to 01. The pin is Brasília, the seat from which the order is conferred; the source names no ceremony venue.
stops.campa: The Brazilian state decorates him. Forty-one years after its army took the government and thirty-four after its agents took him off a São Paulo street, the republic hands the Order of Cultural Merit to a man it tortured. He accepts it. The regime that did the thing is gone, the ministry conferring the order answers to a president the country elected, and the country that outlived the dictatorship is the one his exercises have been addressed to since Penha.

stops.campa: The Prince Claus Fund names him among its laureates for the year, with Patricia Ariza, Emily Jacir, and Faustin Linyekula, who takes the Principal Award for work made out of Kisangani. Boal is seventy-six, and he is cited for the theatre. In the same period he publishes the last of the books, The Aesthetics of the Oppressed, which argues that the point was never to produce theatre and was never to produce politics either, but to give back to people the aesthetic capacity that had been taken off them along with everything else.
stops.quote: We must all do theatre – to find out who we are, and to discover who we could become.
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, The Aesthetics of the Oppressed, trans. Adrian Jackson (Routledge, 2006)

stops.campa: UNESCO names him World Theatre Ambassador. He is seventy-eight and has two months left. The United Nations is naming as an ambassador a man one of its member states took off a street in 1971 and put in a cell. He receives it in the same city where he spent eight years of exile building a centre for a technique which at that point had no institution of any kind behind it. The post carries no theatre and no salary. It is a name for what the method has already become without any state's help.

stops.name: Place de Fontenoy, Paris: the World Theatre Day message
stops.date_confidence: attested from the primary source: the International Theatre Institute's own PDF of the 2009 World Theatre Day message was retrieved and its text extracted, confirming the date. The quotation is carried in full; the gathering pass had cut it after 'in all societies' and closed it with a full stop and no ellipsis, fabricating a sentence boundary.
stops.campa: The International Theatre Institute asks him for the World Theatre Day message, which goes out to every theatre in the world on the twenty-seventh of March. He writes it in the middle of the global financial crisis and he does not write about theatre. He writes about who is being crushed and by what, and then he repeats the thing he has been saying since Buenos Aires, which is that the audience is not an audience. It is his last public statement. Five weeks later he is in intensive care.
stops.quote: When we look beyond appearances, we see oppressors and oppressed people, in all societies, ethnic groups, genders, social classes and casts; we see an unfair and cruel world.
stops.quote_source: Augusto Boal, World Theatre Day Message, International Theatre Institute, 27 March 2009

stops.campa: At about twenty to three in the morning he dies in intensive care on the Rua Bambina, of respiratory failure, with leukaemia. He is seventy-eight. He was born eleven kilometres north of this room and spent fifteen of the years in between forbidden to enter the country. The Centre he founded is a short distance west of here, on the Avenida Mem de Sá, and it opens as usual in the week that follows. Five weeks earlier his World Theatre Day message had been read aloud in playhouses on every continent, which is the widest audience any text of his ever reached.

Outside Brazil the method runs in schools, unions, prisons and refugee camps under people who never met him, in the twenty-five and more languages of the book. There is no statue and no monument. What stands in the place of one is an institution at a street number in Lapa and a technique that spreads only by being used.
